question: Which classical Indian dance form, prevalent in the state of Kerala, reflects an ancient war technique through the use of elaborate colourful make-up and a unique mask?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kathakali.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kathakali is the classical dance-drama of Kerala, instantly recognised by its elaborate green (pacha), red and black facial make-up called chutti, huge headgear and mask-like painted faces.

◦ Its vigorous leaps, stances and footwork are borrowed from the ancient Kerala martial art Kalaripayattu, which is why the form is said to reflect an old war technique.

• Themes are drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas; it is traditionally performed by male artists, accompanied by chenda and maddalam drums.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Kuchipudi — classical dance of Andhra Pradesh, famous for the tarangam (dancing on a brass plate).

• Odissi — of Odisha, known for the tribhanga (three-bend) posture and temple sculpture-like poses.

• Mohiniyattam — of Kerala, a graceful solo lasya dance performed by women in off-white and gold costume.

NOTE

• Eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Kalaripayattu of Kerala is regarded as one of the oldest martial arts in the world.

question: In which country did the game of cricket originate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is England.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cricket originated in England — it grew out of a children's game in the south-east of England (Kent/Sussex, Weald region) in the 16th century and became the national sport by the 18th century.

• The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), founded in 1787, is the custodian of the Laws of Cricket; its home is Lord's, London, called the 'Home of Cricket'.

• The first-ever Test match was played in 1877 between Australia and England at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• India played its first Test in 1932 at Lord's, captained by C. K. Nayudu.

• South Africa was the third Test-playing nation (1889); it was banned during the apartheid era (1970–1991).

• New Zealand played its first Test in 1930.

NOTE

• ICC (International Cricket Council) was founded in 1909 as the Imperial Cricket Conference; headquarters — Dubai, UAE.

• First Cricket World Cup — 1975, won by West Indies; India won in 1983, 2011 (ODI) and 2007, 2024 (T20).

question: ______ is the minimum amount of funds that banks have to keep as a deposit with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cash Reserve Ratio.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is the minimum share of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that it must keep as cash deposits with the RBI.

◦ Banks earn no interest on CRR balances, and it is maintained in cash form only.

• CRR is a quantitative credit-control tool: raising CRR sucks liquidity out of the system (checks inflation), lowering it releases liquidity.

• It is governed by the RBI Act, 1934; the RBI can fix CRR without any floor or ceiling.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) — share of NDTL kept with the bank itself in cash, gold or approved securities (Banking Regulation Act, 1949).

• Repo rate — rate at which RBI lends short-term money to banks against securities; Reverse repo — rate at which RBI borrows from banks.

• Bank rate — long-term lending rate of RBI without collateral; LAF — the repo/reverse-repo window used for day-to-day liquidity management.

NOTE

• RBI was established on 1 April 1935, nationalised on 1 January 1949; headquarters — Mumbai.

• Monetary policy is decided by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) — 6 members, headed by the RBI Governor.

question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for the Advocate-General of the State?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 165.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 165 of the Constitution provides for the Advocate General of the State — the highest law officer of a State.

◦ He/she is appointed by the Governor and must be qualified to be a Judge of a High Court; holds office during the pleasure of the Governor.

• Article 177 allows the Advocate General to speak in and take part in the proceedings of the State Legislature (but not to vote).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Article 136 — Special Leave Petition (SLP) to the Supreme Court.

• Article 145 — Rules of Court, etc., of the Supreme Court.

• Article 77 — Conduct of business of the Government of India.

NOTE

• Article 76 — Attorney General of India, the highest law officer of the Union, appointed by the President.

• The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are statutory/executive posts, not constitutional ones.

question: On the full moon (Purnima) date of which month of the Hindu calendar is Guru Nanak Jayanti celebrated every year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kartik.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Guru Nanak Jayanti (Guru Nanak Gurpurab / Prakash Parv) is celebrated on the full-moon day (Purnima) of the month of Kartik of the Hindu calendar — hence it is also called Kartik Purnima.

• Guru Nanak Dev (born 1469 at Talwandi/Nankana Sahib, now in Pakistan) was the first Sikh Guru and the founder of Sikhism.

• The festival begins with Prabhat Pheris, Akhand Path (48-hour non-stop reading of the Guru Granth Sahib) and Langar.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Vaishakh — month of Baisakhi, when Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa (1699); also Buddha Purnima falls in Vaishakh.

• Chaitra — first month of the Hindu (Vikram Samvat) year; Chaitra Shukla Pratipada marks Gudi Padwa/Ugadi.

• Ashadh — the month of the Jagannath Rath Yatra at Puri and Guru Purnima.

NOTE

• Guru Nanak's core teachings: Naam Japo, Kirat Karo, Vand Chhako; his verses are compiled in the Guru Granth Sahib as 'Japji Sahib'.

• Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth and last human Sikh Guru; he conferred guruship on the Guru Granth Sahib in 1708.

question: Which of the following books is the autobiography of the Dalai Lama?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Freedom in Exile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• 'Freedom in Exile' (1990) is the autobiography of the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism.

• It narrates his early life in Tibet, the Chinese takeover, and his escape to India in 1959, after which he set up the Tibetan government-in-exile at Dharamshala (McLeodganj), Himachal Pradesh.

• The Dalai Lama was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 and India's Bharat Ratna has not been given to him, though he received the Templeton Prize (2012).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• 'Playing It My Way' (2014) — autobiography of cricketer Sachin Tendulkar.

• 'Touch Play' (1999) — autobiography of tennis player Mahesh Bhupathi (co-authored).

• 'Red Sari' (The Red Sari) — a fictionalised biography of Sonia Gandhi by Spanish author Javier Moro.

NOTE

• Other autobiography of the Dalai Lama: 'My Land and My People' (1962); other works — 'The Art of Happiness', 'Ethics for the New Millennium'.

• Frequently asked pairs: 'Wings of Fire' — A. P. J. Abdul Kalam; 'My Experiments with Truth' — Mahatma Gandhi; 'An Autobiography' — Jawaharlal Nehru.

question: Which Turkish invader attacked the Somnath temple in 1025 AD?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahmud of Ghazni.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mahmud of Ghazni (ruled 998–1030 AD), the Turkish ruler of the Ghaznavid dynasty, attacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat in 1025 AD and plundered its enormous wealth.

• He is said to have invaded India 17 times between 1000 and 1027 AD, mainly for wealth, not for territory.

• His court had scholars such as Firdausi (author of *Shahnama*) and Al-Beruni (author of *Kitab-ul-Hind/Tahqiq-i-Hind*).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Muhammad Ghori — defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the Second Battle of Tarain (1192); laid the foundation of Muslim rule in India.

• Muhammad bin Qasim — Arab general who conquered Sindh in 712 AD, defeating Raja Dahir.

• Muhammad bin Tughlaq — Delhi Sultan (1325–51) known for transferring the capital to Daulatabad and issuing token currency.

NOTE

• The Somnath temple, on the Saurashtra coast of Gujarat, is the first among the twelve Jyotirlingas; it was rebuilt after Independence at the initiative of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (1951).

• Mahmud's most famous battle in India was against Jayapala and Anandapala of the Hindu Shahi dynasty.

question: According to the Human Development Index (HDI) Report 2021-22, which country performed best among the countries of the Indian subcontinent?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sri Lanka.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the UNDP Human Development Report 2021-22 ('Uncertain Times, Unsettled Lives', released September 2022), Sri Lanka ranked 73rd with an HDI value of about 0.782 — the best in the Indian subcontinent.

• India ranked 132 out of 191 countries with an HDI of 0.633, in the 'medium human development' category.

• HDI is a composite of three dimensions — health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean & expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Bhutan — rank 127; Bangladesh — rank 129; Nepal — rank 143 in the same report.

• Switzerland topped the 2021-22 HDI, followed by Norway and Iceland; South Sudan was last.

NOTE

• The HDI was devised in 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistan) and Amartya Sen (India); it is published by the UNDP.

• HDI value ranges from 0 to 1; categories — Low (<0.550), Medium (0.550–0.699), High (0.700–0.799), Very High (≥0.800).

question: Dachigam National Park is located in which of the following States/Union Territories?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jammu and Kashmir.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Dachigam National Park lies about 22 km from Srinagar in the union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, in the Zabarwan range of the western Himalayas.

• It is the last natural home of the Hangul (Kashmir stag), the state animal of Jammu and Kashmir — a critically endangered species.

• The name 'Dachigam' literally means 'ten villages', referring to the ten villages relocated when the area was created (1910) to protect Srinagar's water supply; it became a national park in 1981.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Gujarat — Gir National Park (Asiatic lion), Blackbuck (Velavadar), Marine and Vansda National Parks.

• Karnataka — Bandipur, Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi), Bannerghatta, Anshi and Kudremukh National Parks.

• Kerala — Periyar, Eravikulam (Nilgiri tahr), Silent Valley and Anamudi Shola National Parks.

NOTE

• Other protected areas of J&K/Ladakh: Kishtwar, Salim Ali and Hemis (largest national park in India, in Ladakh — snow leopard).

• India's first national park — Hailey National Park (1936), now Jim Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand.

question: Which temple is also known as the Black Pagoda?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sun Temple, Konark.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Konark Sun Temple in Odisha is popularly called the 'Black Pagoda' — a name given by European sailors because of its dark, towering silhouette which served as a landmark on the Bay of Bengal coast.

• It was built in the 13th century (c. 1250 AD) by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, in the Kalinga style of Nagara architecture.

• The temple is designed as the chariot of Surya with 24 carved wheels and 7 horses; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Jagannath Temple is at Puri (not Hyderabad) and is called the 'White Pagoda'.

• The Somnath Temple, Saurashtra (Gujarat), is the first of the twelve Jyotirlingas.

• The Omkareshwar Temple is on Mandhata island in the Narmada river, Madhya Pradesh — also a Jyotirlinga.

NOTE

• Other famous Sun temples: Modhera (Gujarat, Solanki king Bhimdev I), Martand (Kashmir, Lalitaditya Muktapida), Dakshinaarka (Gaya).

• Konark hosts the annual Konark Dance Festival; the wheels of the temple appear on the Indian ₹10 note.

question: White light is composed of how many colours?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Seven.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• White light (sunlight) is made up of seven colours — VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

• The splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism is called dispersion, first demonstrated by Sir Isaac Newton (1666).

◦ Dispersion occurs because different colours have different wavelengths and hence different refractive indices — violet bends the most, red the least.

• Recombining the spectrum with a second inverted prism gives back white light; a rapidly rotating Newton's disc also appears white.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Red has the longest wavelength (~700 nm) and lowest frequency; violet the shortest (~400 nm) and highest frequency.

• A rainbow is formed by dispersion, refraction and total internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets — red on the outside, violet inside (primary rainbow).

NOTE

• Primary colours of light — Red, Green, Blue (RGB); primary pigments — Cyan, Magenta, Yellow.

• The blue colour of the sky and the red colour of the setting sun are due to scattering of light (Rayleigh scattering), not dispersion.

question: A settlement of closely built dwellings, found wherever flat land is available, is called a ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Compact settlement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A compact (nucleated/clustered) settlement is one in which houses are built close to one another wherever flat, fertile land is available.

• Such settlements develop in river valleys and fertile plains where farming is intensive, water is available, and people cluster for security and social cooperation — e.g. the Ganga plains.

• The opposite is a dispersed/scattered settlement, found in hills, forests and dry regions where houses are few and far apart.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Linear settlement — houses arranged in a line along a road, railway, canal, river bank or valley.

• Scattered/dispersed settlement — isolated huts spread over a wide area, typical of plateaus, deserts and hilly tracts.

• Other shapes: circular/semi-circular (around lakes/ponds), star-shaped (where several roads meet), rectangular/grid and T, Y, cross-shaped.

NOTE

• Settlements are broadly classified as rural (agriculture-based) and urban (secondary/tertiary activity based).

• Transhumance settlements are temporary/seasonal, used by migratory herders.

question: M. S. Gopalakrishnan had mastered both Carnatic and Hindustani classical music. He was a skilled ______ player.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Violin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• M. S. Gopalakrishnan (1931–2013), popularly called MSG, was a legendary Indian violinist who had mastered both Carnatic and Hindustani classical styles.

• He belonged to the celebrated Parur school (bani) of violin playing, trained by his father Parur Sundaram Iyer.

• He was honoured with the Padma Shri (1976), Padma Bhushan (2012) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1976).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Sitar — Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee.

• Sarangi — Ram Narayan, Sultan Khan, Bundu Khan.

• Santoor — Shivkumar Sharma, Bhajan Sopori (a Kashmiri instrument).

NOTE

• Other famous violinists: L. Subramaniam, T. N. Krishnan, N. Rajam, Kunnakudi Vaidyanathan.

• Instruments classified as string (tata) — sitar, sarod, violin, santoor, veena; wind (sushir) — flute, shehnai, nadaswaram; percussion (avanaddha) — tabla, mridangam, pakhawaj.

question: The southern part of India lies within the ______ zone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tropical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Tropic of Cancer (23°30' N) passes almost through the middle of India, dividing it into two halves — the part south of it lies in the tropical zone, and the part north of it in the sub-tropical/temperate zone.

• The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.

• Because of this location, southern India has high temperatures throughout the year with little seasonal variation, while northern India shows extremes.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The temperate zone lies between the Tropic and the Arctic/Antarctic Circle (23.5° – 66.5°).

• The frigid/polar zone lies beyond 66.5° latitude — the Arctic and Antarctic regions.

• 'Rainfall' is not a climatic zone at all; it is an element of climate.

NOTE

• India's mainland extends from 8°4' N to 37°6' N latitude and 68°7' E to 97°25' E longitude.

• The standard meridian of India is 82°30' E, passing through Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh); IST = GMT + 5:30 hours.

question: When did the Second Battle of Tarain take place?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1192.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Second Battle of Tarain (1192 AD) was fought between Muhammad Ghori and Prithviraj Chauhan III, in which Ghori decisively defeated the Rajput ruler.

• Tarain (Taraori) lies near Thanesar in present-day Haryana.

• This victory broke Rajput resistance in north India and laid the foundation of Turkish/Muslim rule in India; Ghori's slave Qutb-ud-din Aibak later founded the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• First Battle of Tarain (1191) — Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad Ghori.

• 1175 AD — Muhammad Ghori's first Indian campaign, the conquest of Multan.

• Battle of Chandawar (1194) — Ghori defeated Jaichandra of Kannauj (Gahadavala dynasty).

NOTE

• Prithviraj Raso, written by Chand Bardai, is the epic poem on Prithviraj Chauhan.

• Delhi Sultanate dynasties in order: Slave (1206), Khilji (1290), Tughlaq (1320), Sayyid (1414), Lodi (1451–1526).

question: India first participated in the Olympics in the year ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1900.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India first participated in the Olympic Games at the 1900 Paris Olympics, represented by a single athlete, Norman Pritchard.

• Pritchard won two silver medals — in the 200 m sprint and the 200 m hurdles — India's first-ever Olympic medals.

• India sent its first official team in 1920 (Antwerp Olympics); the Indian Olympic Association was formed in 1927.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• India's men's hockey team won its first Olympic gold at Amsterdam 1928 and took 8 golds in all (last in Moscow 1980).

• KD Jadhav won India's first individual Olympic medal (wrestling bronze) at Helsinki 1952.

• Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual Olympic gold (10 m air rifle) at Beijing 2008.

NOTE

• The modern Olympics began in 1896 at Athens, revived by Pierre de Coubertin; the IOC is headquartered at Lausanne, Switzerland.

• Olympic motto — 'Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter' (Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together).

question: In which Census of India were transgender persons' statistics officially collected and recorded for the first time?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2011.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Census of India 2011 was the first census to officially collect and record data on transgender persons, by providing an 'Other' category besides male and female.

• It recorded about 4.88 lakh (4,87,803) transgender persons in the country.

• Census 2011 was the 15th National Census of India and the 7th after Independence; its slogan was 'Our Census, Our Future'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Census 2011 data: population 121.08 crore, sex ratio 943, literacy 74.04%, density 382 persons/sq km.

• Most populous state — Uttar Pradesh; least — Sikkim; highest literacy — Kerala; lowest — Bihar.

• Highest sex ratio — Kerala (1084); lowest — Haryana (879).

NOTE

• The first census in India was conducted in 1872 under Lord Mayo; the first complete/synchronous census in 1881 under Lord Ripon.

• The NALSA v. Union of India (2014) judgment recognised transgender persons as the 'third gender'; the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019.

question: Which State Government launched India's first elephant death audit framework?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tamil Nadu.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Tamil Nadu became the first State in India to introduce an elephant death audit framework, to scientifically record and investigate every elephant death in the State.

• Under it, every elephant death is documented with post-mortem, photographs and cause analysis, and unnatural deaths (electrocution, train hits, poaching, poisoning) are reviewed to fix accountability.

• Tamil Nadu has a large elephant population and several elephant reserves such as Nilgiri, Coimbatore, Anamalai and Srivilliputhur.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Project Elephant was launched in 1992 by the Government of India for the protection of elephants, their habitat and corridors.

• The Indian elephant is listed as Endangered in the IUCN Red List and placed in Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

• The elephant was declared India's National Heritage Animal in 2010.

NOTE

• Karnataka has the highest elephant population in India, followed by Assam and Kerala.

• World Elephant Day is observed on 12 August.

question: Which of the following is a complex permanent plant tissue?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Xylem.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Xylem is a complex permanent tissue — it is made of more than one type of cell (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres) which work together as a unit.

• Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves and also gives mechanical support.

• The other complex permanent tissue is phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres), which transports food in both directions.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Apical meristem and lateral meristem are meristematic (dividing) tissues, not permanent tissues — apical causes growth in length, lateral (cambium) in girth.

• Collenchyma is a simple permanent tissue (single cell type) that gives flexibility to young stems and leaf stalks.

NOTE

• Simple permanent tissues — parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex permanent tissues — xylem and phloem.

• Aerenchyma (parenchyma with air cavities) helps aquatic plants float; chlorenchyma contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis.

question: 'The Stars in My Sky: Those Who Brightened My Film Journey' is the second book of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Divya Dutta.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• 'The Stars in My Sky: Those Who Brightened My Film Journey' is the second book of Bollywood actress Divya Dutta.

• In it she writes affectionate portraits of the actors, directors and co-stars who shaped her career in the film industry.

• Her first book was the memoir 'Me and Ma' (2017), dedicated to her mother.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Divya Dutta won the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actress for 'Irada' (2017); other notable films — *Veer-Zaara*, *Bhaag Milkha Bhaag*, *Delhi-6*.

• Neeti Mohan is a well-known playback singer, not an author of this book.

• Amitabh Bachchan and Sonam Kapoor are actors, not the authors of this book.

NOTE

• Other well-known Bollywood books: 'An Unsuitable Boy' — Karan Johar; 'The Substance and the Shadow' — Dilip Kumar; 'Romancing with Life' — Dev Anand.

• Remember the pair for exams: Divya Dutta — 'Me and Ma' (first book) and 'The Stars in My Sky' (second book).

question: The average salinity of the ocean is ______ parts per thousand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 35.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The average salinity of ocean water is 35 parts per thousand (35‰ or 35 ppt) — i.e. 35 grams of dissolved salts in every 1,000 grams (1 litre) of sea water.

• The most abundant salt is sodium chloride (common salt), which makes up about 77% of the dissolved solids.

• Salinity depends on evaporation, precipitation, river inflow, ice formation/melting and ocean currents; it is highest in the sub-tropical high-pressure belts.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Lake Van (Turkey) has the highest salinity (~330‰), followed by the Dead Sea (~238‰) and the Great Salt Lake, Utah.

• Among seas, the Red Sea has the highest salinity (~41‰); the Baltic Sea the lowest (~7‰) because of heavy river inflow and low evaporation.

NOTE

• Salinity is measured in parts per thousand (ppt/‰) or PSU (Practical Salinity Unit).

• Water containing more than 24.7‰ salinity is termed 'brackish/salt water' for oceanographic purposes; the Arabian Sea is more saline than the Bay of Bengal because the latter receives huge river discharge.

question: What is the primary objective of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)?
option_1: To control the number of malaria cases
solution_text:
The correct answer is to control air pollution.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is a set of emergency anti-air-pollution measures for Delhi-NCR, which are triggered in stages as the Air Quality Index (AQI) worsens.

• It was notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in 2017, following a Supreme Court order; it is now implemented by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).

• GRAP has four stages — Stage I 'Poor' (AQI 201–300), Stage II 'Very Poor' (301–400), Stage III 'Severe' (401–450) and Stage IV 'Severe Plus' (above 450) — with progressively stricter curbs such as banning construction, diesel generators, trucks and even school closures.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), launched in 2019, aims to reduce particulate pollution in over 130 non-attainment cities.

• AQI in India (launched 2014, 'Ek Number') has six categories: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400), Severe (401–500).

NOTE

• Odd-Even scheme and the Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI) fuel norms (2020) are other measures against vehicular pollution.

• The CPCB (Central Pollution Control Board) was set up in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act.

question: Who among the following led the Chittagong Armoury Raid?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Surya Sen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Chittagong Armoury Raid of 18 April 1930 was led by Surya Sen, popularly called 'Masterda' because he was a school teacher.

• His revolutionary group, the Indian Republican Army (Chittagong branch), seized the police and auxiliary force armouries and hoisted the national flag, proclaiming a provisional revolutionary government.

• Associates included Ganesh Ghosh, Ambika Chakrabarty, Lokenath Bal, Anant Singh, Pritilata Waddedar and Kalpana Dutta. Surya Sen was captured in 1933 and hanged on 12 January 1934.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Rabindranath Tagore — poet, first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913); renounced his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh (1919).

• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — leader of the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) and architect of the integration of princely states.

• V. D. Savarkar — founder of Abhinav Bharat, author of 'The Indian War of Independence 1857', transported to the Cellular Jail, Andaman.

NOTE

• Pritilata Waddedar led the attack on the Pahartali European Club (1932) and is remembered as one of India's first women revolutionary martyrs.

• Other revolutionary actions: Kakori Conspiracy (1925), Central Assembly Bomb Case (1929), Lahore Conspiracy Case (1929–31).

question: Who among the following freedom fighters is called the 'Father of Modern India'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833) is called the 'Father of Modern India' and the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance' for pioneering social and religious reform.

• He founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815), the Brahmo Sabha (1828) — later the Brahmo Samaj — and campaigned successfully for the abolition of Sati in 1829 with Lord William Bentinck.

• He championed English and modern scientific education, women's rights, widow remarriage and the freedom of the press; the Mughal emperor Akbar II conferred on him the title 'Raja'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Swami Vivekananda — disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahansa, founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897); famous Chicago address at the Parliament of Religions, 1893.

• Keshab Chandra Sen — Brahmo leader who later formed the Brahmo Samaj of India; associated with the Native Marriage Act, 1872.

• Baba Dayal Das — founder of the Nirankari movement among Sikhs.

NOTE

• Roy published newspapers/journals — Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali), Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian) and 'Brahmanical Magazine'.

• He died at Bristol, England, in 1833; Debendranath Tagore and later Keshab Chandra Sen carried the Brahmo Samaj forward.

question: According to the Constitution of India, who is the head of the Indian Union?
solution_text:
The correct answer is the President of India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under Article 52, 'There shall be a President of India'; the President is the constitutional head of the Indian Union (State) and the first citizen of the country.

• Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, exercised by him directly or through officers subordinate to him.

• The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college consisting of elected MPs and elected MLAs of States and of Delhi & Puducherry, by the system of proportional representation with a single transferable vote (Article 54–55). Term — 5 years.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The Prime Minister is the real/executive head of the government and head of the Council of Ministers (Article 74–75).

• The Vice-President (Article 63) is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and acts as President in case of a vacancy.

• The Chief Justice of India heads the judiciary and administers the oath of office to the President (Article 60).

NOTE

• Minimum age to become President — 35 years; the President is also the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.

• Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President; Droupadi Murmu assumed office in 2022 as the 15th President and the first from a tribal community.
